articles.title: The Big Beautiful Boycott: Starbucks Workers’ Fight for a First Contract
articles.author: Ian M.
articles.content: After five years of strikes, marches on the boss, petitions, and legal action, Starbucks Workers United (SBWU) called for a boycott in August. Beyond individual coffee drinkers, the union is asking universities, other unions, candidates, and political organizations to sign on to the boycott campaign. Boycotts have a long history in the labor movement but can be risky. They rely on external support, and if they fail to make a dent in the company’s bottom line, they risk undercutting the momentum of the movement. Luckily for SBWU, unions are more popular than ever, and we’ve already seen that plenty of people are ready to throw down to support their baristas. Since 2021, Starbucks workers have been organizing at an impressive rate. Anyone who pays any attention to the labor movement has heard about the rank-and-file energy that has led over 12,000 workers at almost 700 stores to organize unions. This is a movement built on bottom-up militancy. Through a pandemic, two presidencies, four CEOs, and intense company offensives, Starbucks workers have soldiered on. Carried by the energy of the Bernie campaign, Black Lives Matter Movement, and Covid strike wave, the union has continued to grow rapidly. And at key inflection points, it has risen to the political moment, beginning with the labor-friendly Biden administration. Its National Labor Relations Board fast-tracked elections and frequently issued fines and injunctions against the company, helped, but it was reverberations of these consciousness-raising mass movements that actually inspired the workers. According to Eric Blanc’s We Are The Union , in 2022, more than 25% of leaders of new union drives cited BLM, Bernie Sanders, LGBTQ rights, or climate as the primary inspiration for their work. And in October 2023, soon after Israel launched its genocidal campaign in Gaza, SBWU became one of the first unions in the US to call for a ceasefire. Immediately, the company filed a lawsuit, alleging that SBWU was harming its image. The result was an organic consumer boycott so widespread that, in conjunction with a 2024 holiday-season strike at more than 300 stores and several student-led pressure campaigns that cut university contracts with Starbucks, it brought the company to the bargaining table for the first time. Initially, workers secured 33 tentative agreements on a number of issues, but with Trump and his counter-revolution coming to power, the writing was on the wall. The company would walk away in 2025. The 2025 Strike In 2025, while new stores were still organizing, the company was unyielding. That summer, SBWU set about building a strike big enough to make a real dent. Workers started organizing both internally and externally. While stores elected strike captains, the union worked to build a strong network of supporters who could bolster picket lines and take solidarity actions. Reaching out to both individuals and groups, SBWU and DSA came to work closely. DSA, through its National Labor Commission (NLC), already had a strong system of Solidarity Captains. These members were point people in their chapters, with the know-how and the support to activate their comrades in support of workers’ struggles. We on the NLC worked to connect DSA solidarity captains to their local SBWU strike captains and built our own muscles in anticipation of a strike. SBWU often chooses to launch national strikes on Red Cup Day, when Starbucks unveils its limited-edition holiday-themed cup. Every November, it proves to be the company’s highest sales day of the year. Having a concrete timeline was unusual and helpful for DSA. We were able to prepare captains ahead of time with all the information they needed, as well as a variety of support tactics chapters could use. Using DSA’s Labor Solidarity Fund, the Labor Commission ensured that chapters had banners, megaphones, tents, and anything else they might need to support the picket lines. We even worked with a socialist chef to create a strike kitchen menu, enabling over a dozen DSA and YDSA chapters to bring good, hot food to the lines . In Pennsylvania and Nevada, DSA and YDSA chapters mobilized to support mass picketing outside Starbucks’ regional distribution facilities, disrupting shipments of beans and other key supplies across the Northeast and Southwest. For the six-week duration of the strike, over 100 DSA chapters were mobilized. Whether supporting picket lines or talking to baristas and customers at nonunion stores, our nationwide strength was on display. While the company claimed there was no effect on its bottom line, the union’s estimates suggested differently. New stores were inspired to organize. The movement grew. But the company did not fold. A few months later, SBWU returned to the bargaining table after submitting a new, lower wage proposal. Since then, the two sides have been bargaining off and on. The Boycott Now Since August 25th, for the first time, workers themselves are calling on customers to avoid all corporately owned Starbucks locations and products. This means stand-alone brick and mortar stores (excluding those in Target stores, airports, etc.), as well as Starbucks products in grocery stores. Though it’s not yet clear exactly how the boycott will fit in a larger strategy to win a contract, it does build on SBWU’s strengths. To get the word out, Starbucks workers have continued to skillfully use social media, which was critical in the movement’s initial growth. The boycott also functions as an effective structure test for the union: it can test its relationships with other organizations and with elected officials. The first stage of the boycott campaign included reaching out to unions and progressive organizations, including DSA, to pass resolutions in support and ban Starbucks products from their events, encouraging others to join. City councils in Atlanta , St. Louis , and Philadelphia have passed boycott resolutions, and Austin DSA members are now using their positions on the city council to fight for their own. Politicians like NYC DSA’s Claire Valdez have spoken publicly supporting the boycott and for the council to change procurement rules to prevent the city from buying Starbucks products. Undoubtedly, building the boycott will require some action in the real world. While the union isn’t taking many of these steps yet, DSAers should be prepared to organize informational events and rallies alongside baristas in order to spread the word. In some places, we already have a good model. Louisville DSA organized a solidarity rally with SBWU members in early September. According to organizer Galen Z.S., nearly 40 union siblings and DSA members came out in 100+ degree heat to occupy a strip of grass outside a Starbucks. Since that store was having its election a week later, the rally was an opportunity to demonstrate solidarity in the face of intense union-busting. (Though in the end, intimidation and threats led to an 8-7 loss.) Rallies like this one are an example of the multifaceted strategy necessary to take down Starbucks. Worker action on the shop floor can occur alongside local advocacy groups, faith communities, and allies in other unions. When CEO Brian Niccol sees an unbroken wall of social opposition to drinking Starbucks coffee and 12,000+ union baristas acting in concert on the shop floor, the power built will be formidable. What Will It Take? Starbucks is a massive company. While SBWU represents more than 700 stores, there are over 10,000 corporately owned Starbucks locations in the United States. There are many thousands more workers to organize and elections to win, but a contract could be won before then. Whether it’s necessary to settle for a less lucrative first contract to temper company opposition or win a stronger contract to show workers that their organizing was worth it is still an open question . Either outcome depends on the ability to keep applying pressure through frequent shop floor actions, effective strikes, and a mass boycott movement. All this must contend with high turnover: at many unionized stores, it’s not uncommon to see an entirely new set of workers just a year after an election. Socialists have much to learn from this organizing drive, and an important role to play if it is going to succeed. While Starbucks may not be the “commanding heights of industry,” SBWU is a real breakthrough in organizing the service sector, a large and growing portion of the U.S. economy. And Starbucks organizing drives have had a “spillover effect,” inspiring workers in other nearby workplaces to organize themselves. According to a study from Colorado State, nearly 20% of the nationwide increase in union elections since 2021 can be attributed to Starbucks organizing drive “spillovers,” with counties that saw Starbucks elections showing a 175% increase in union elections. And while union baristas don’t always stick around for long, they will take their class struggle experience with them for the rest of their lives. articles.title: An Effective AI Pushback Has to Go Beyond the Local
articles.author: Aziz Huq
articles.content: Last week’s election returns embodied a broad, national, and bipartisan reaction against data centers. In forty-six of the forty-seven local referenda held across some thirteen states, voters rejected new data center construction. Public opposition reflects local concerns about water usage, grid sustainability, and noise pollution. This opposition is also bubbling up at a moment when most of the public distrust s artificial intelligence (AI) in general, when two-thirds of Americans hold negative views of AI firms and their close ties to the Trump administration, and when fears about AI rank high among Americans’ leading worries. This confluence of AI-adjacent fears is no accident. Each anxious spark leaps from a different facet of a single Silicon Valley strategy for hyperscaling AI. If this strategy works, it would induce a dramatic decline in labor’s income share of income. If it fails, it would saddle the state with crushing mountains of debt. Voters, to be sure, likely perceive this dilemma only weakly. Yet their vivid fears create a chance for the Left to articulate a comprehensive diagnosis of hyperscale AI’s manifold problems — one that not only affirms the public’s fears but also articulates a coherent response. And just as the Silicon Valley strategy runs on a logic of scale, so too an effectual pushback must escalate beyond the local. Heads, AI Wins. Tails, You Lose. Generative AI is being developed by a small handful of firms. They are taking on massive amounts of debt to build computing power on which costly new tools can be offered at scale. Given the size of these investments, the firms are commercially viable only if they sell their wares at scale. This means either tapping hidden wellsprings of productivity growth ( unlikely ) or being used as a low-marginal-cost substitute for white-collar labor (more likely). The ensuing debt-fueled displacement of white-collar labor, if successful, will induce a massive shift of income from labor to capital, as even the AI firms concede . The ruination of ecosystems and acceleration of the climate crisis are mere side effects. There is strong historical evidence of technology’s corrosive effect on the labor share: recent data from Europe suggests that AI, no less than other recent tech leaps, causes losses to labor and corresponding gains to capital. Worse, because most democracies tax capital at lower rates than labor, that shift will constrict the state, diminishing its fiscal capacity to cushion job losses and declining wages. In effect, hyperscale AI creates a distributional crisis and robs the state of tools to address it. Of course, this strategy might not work. AI might not be transformative as its boosters claim. Markets may lose their nerve before profits can be reaped. But if the AI strategy isn’t successful, the leading firms now dominant in public equity markets (and hence our pensions and 401[k]s), will almost certainly demand a “rescue” akin to the 2008–9 federal financial-crisis interventions. As of August, hyperscale AI firms had accrued more than $500 million in debt from private equity, banks, and institutional investors such as Blackrock and Pimco. If that debt sours, the repercussions of the crisis, as in 2008–9, would likely force the government’s hand. If that happens, a massive transfer of risk to public balance sheets will follow. This is capitalism as a “heads I win, tails you lose” proposition. Whether or not it founders, hyperscale AI capitalism will cleave open immense lost opportunities for society at large. On one estimate , US AI investments will add up to some $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032, or an average of 3.63 percent of US gross domestic product per year. This is $10 trillion that will not and cannot be spend on maternal care, pre-K education, cancer treatment, environmental mitigation, or any other social programs and planetary reparative work we desperately need. It is, by any measure, a staggering divergence of investment away from areas of urgent moral priority. No wonder, then, that the American public has such profound anxieties. The data center build-outs are simply the most apparent of the many economic, political, fiscal, and environmental crises that hyperscale AI is inducing. Building Toward a National Response What then might be an effectual response? Except in Harwood, North Dakota, voters have pushed back at a local level by denying construction permission, or in Perry, Ohio, demanding that firms post a bond as insurance against the risk of fiscal implosion. Localities’ responses are circumscribed, though, by their limited powers and their small geographic reach. Cities and counties can do little about the labor market effects or fiscal risk. Many environmental costs associated with new demands on the electric grid are out of their reach. Some cities such as Austin and San Antonio own and operate their own electrical utilities, giving them a lever that doesn’t exist elsewhere in the country. But these are exceptions. Solely local responses are usually tightly constrained. Since the effects of hyperscale AI capitalism emerge at the national level, it would ideally be the federal government that drives a comprehensive response. Pessimism about the prospect of federal action is wise for now. After Tuesday’s election, Trump reiterated his belief that data centers are “gold . . . only foolish leadership will say NO.” His December 2025 executive order , barring states from regulating AI, remains in force, although the legal theories upon which it rests are flawed. Even if a Democratic-controlled House and Senate can overcome his veto, any resulting AI legislation will likely be weak thanks to the need to assemble supermajorities to ensure bills’ passage. The difficulty of federal action, however, does not mean that progressives should give up addressing hyperscale AI capitalism. They still have ways to use both their control at the state level and at the regional level to highlight its costsand offer the beginnings of a commensurate response — indeed, one that might be fully nationalized in two years. In January, Democrats will have “trifectas” in twenty-two states and hold the governor’s office in seven more (Kansas and Alaska are still not called as I write). This is a first platform for action. To date, states’ responses have been reactive and purely negative: New York’s and Oregon’s governors paused data center construction, while laws imposing moratoria have been introduced but not passed in sixteen states. Advocates of successful local ballot initiatives have indicated that they plan to turn to bans in their states. Yet a pause is not a policy. It does nothing to communicate the complex and interconnected harms of hyperscale AI capitalism. So it leaves the field open for AI’s advocates to advance their tall tales of illimitable gain. Nor does it prevent the building of data centers elsewhere in the nation and so does nothing to rein in its fiscal and labor costs. An alternate approach would be for states to force tech firms to not just account for the local effects of data centers but also recognize and take responsibility for all the social costs of their hyperscale strategy. It would seek to channel economic development into less costly, more decent forms. Bans, however, are a badly formed tool to this subtle end. As a start, states could recognize their own complicity in hyperscale AI. In forty states, data centers benefit from exemptions from the sales and use taxes that would ordinarily accrue on building materials, machinery, and equipment. The nominal justification for such exemptions is the jobs new builds purportedly bring. But a data center at best tends to create only two or three hundred jobs, with no long-term effect on wages. Where a landlord like Equinix, Data Realty, or CyrusOne rents computing power to remote clients, even that meager gain goes unrealized. States’ and localities’ ensuing revenue loss is hard to measure , because only some of the states with these tax exemptions report their fiscal effect. Texas, however, lost some $1 billion in FY2025; in 2024, Illinois lost $370 million; and Arizona lost $19 million. A simple first step is terminating all these tax exemptions on the ground that the local benefits from data centers have been illusory, following Maine’s example. That might also prompt states to reconsider more generally their blind pursuit of corporate investments through tax relief. Having withdrawn their reckless subsidies, states should follow Perry, Ohio’s lead by forcing tech firms to bear the social costs of their speculative investments. New construction, for example, might be conditioned on bonds tied to the environmental and state-level labor market effects of their business models. Firms would first be required to report not only on expected environmental harms (including from increased energy demand) but also address whether a data center’s expected uses will displace human labor or otherwise have wage-suppressive effects (as a leading study has already found). It would then have to post bonds sufficient to pay for state investments to buffer those effects. The law might impel an AI-funded guarantee fund to sustain state unemployment payouts and retraining costs generated by AI. States could also require that data center investments be backed by sufficient nondebt financing to mitigate any risk of catastrophic fiscal events. And even if data centers are not fully banned, states might simply target specific uses as verboten — say, the large-scale automation of American jobs. Firms that flout this would see their centers shut down. At the same time, states need not act alone. An underappreciated part of the American constitutional order is groups of states’ latent authority to enter into binding “ compacts .” These are treaty-like agreements, often created without Congress’s approval, to coordinate regulation between a pool of states. Existing compacts address drivers’ licenses, insurance coverage, and medical practice. They allow states to set uniform standards and realize regulation at scale, even if the national government is AWOL. Imagine Texas, Virginia, California, Pennsylvania, and New York forging an interstate compact on AI and data centers. No firm would be permitted to operate data centers in any state unless they agreed to meet certain environmental standards and avoid use cases that threatened serious job loss. The compacting states could require a common set of disclosures — not only about the data centers themselves but also about the fiscal and labor market risks associated with AI more generally, and perhaps about other AI-related harms. Unlike simple bans, this arrangement is more likely to be politically self-sustaining. Firms would, in effect, have to document on an ongoing basis the knot of harms that flow from hyperscale AI — hence supplying the grounds for their own regulation. And they could not simply blame states for quashing economic growth. A race to the bottom as firms tried to pit states against each other would be more difficult. It is true that hyperscale AI capitalists are likely to flee from compacting states. But notice that the creation of a robust compact would limit their flight options, at least within the United States. To see this, consider the political costs to a red state governor who welcomes fleeing data centers that decline to comply with environmental and labor market protections. Recall that some 89 percent of Americans oppose data center siting near them. Isn’t it likely that the governor will meet the same fate as other erstwhile champions of AI, such as outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott? Compacting to clarify AI’s harms makes it politically more difficult for noncompacting states to embrace the industry. No doubt, these solutions are incomplete. But they offer a pathway for dealing with not just the local but also the national harms of hyperscale AI in a politically durable way. They not only signal clearly that voters’ concerns have been heard but also help build virtuous circles of disclosure, action, and revenue so the perils of hyperscale AI can be enduringly addressed — a groundwork that offers a foundation for national action when the time is right. articles.content: Moira’s Parish of Seeds had been born from the bones of a megachurch that was once known for its large and loud worship sessions. articles.title: Metro DC DSA Condemns Councilmember Christina Henderson’s Attempted Power Grab and Disregard for DC Home Rule
articles.author: Metro DC DSA
articles.content: Metro DC DSA Condemns Councilmember Christina Henderson’s Attempted Power Grab and Disregard for DC Home Rule Date: November 8, 2026 Media Contact: For all press inquiries, please contact media@mdcdsa.org . Washington, DC: Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America condemns At-Large Councilmember Christina Henderson’s cynical attempt to manipulate the District’s Home Rule laws for her own political advantage, undermining the democratic process and distracting from the urgent challenges facing working-class Washingtonians. Details: In 2020, Henderson switched her party affiliation from Democrat to independent to run for an At-Large Council seat. Now, following Councilmember Robert White’s resignation, Henderson attempted to reverse that decision, potentially depriving the DC Democratic Party of its authority to appoint an interim replacement and shifting that power to the DC Council. When the DC Democratic Party moved to exercise its appointment authority, selecting Jamal Holtz before Henderson’s registration change took effect, Henderson raised the prospect of legal action. Only after her maneuver failed did she reverse course and re-register as an independent. Analysis: Home Rule is not a political tool to be invoked when convenient and discarded when inconvenient. It is the foundation of the District’s limited right to govern itself, a right generations of Washingtonians have fought to secure against congressional interference. Henderson’s actions have all the appearances of a naked political power grab, seemingly designed to strengthen her position for a potential challenge to the Council chairmanship. Whatever her ambitions, Washingtonians deserve better than elected officials exploiting party registration rules to advance their political careers. This spectacle is particularly offensive at a moment when DC residents face an escalating affordability crisis. Working families are struggling with rising rents, the cost of groceries, and underfunded public services. Instead of addressing these urgent needs, Henderson has manufactured a political controversy over who gets to fill a temporary vacancy on the Council. The timing could hardly be worse. As the District enters a new political era, with renewed threats to our autonomy and an expanded National Guard presence in our streets, our elected officials should be demonstrating the seriousness and resolve necessary to defend DC residents against federal interference. Instead, Henderson’s political maneuvering makes our local government appear unserious, irresponsible, and consumed by personal ambition. Bottom Line: The irony of Henderson invoking Home Rule to defend her actions should not be lost on anyone. The District’s right to self-government belongs to its residents, not to politicians seeking to manipulate the rules for personal advantage. The DC Democratic Party’s authority to appoint an interim replacement is established under District law, and voters will have the opportunity to elect their next At-Large Councilmember in a special election. Metro DC DSA supports respecting the established appointment process while reaffirming our commitment to full DC statehood, which would eliminate the undemocratic congressional restrictions on our local government that helped create this controversy. Councilmember Henderson should abandon these political games and return her attention to the people she was elected to serve. Washingtonians need leaders fighting for affordable housing, strong public schools, fully funded public services, and genuine democratic self-determination, not politicians more interested in their next promotion than the needs of their constituents. Our city deserves a government that takes itself seriously, respects the will of its voters, and puts working people first. articles.title: End the Private Health Insurance Tax: Pass Medicare for All
articles.author: Tim Higginbotham
articles.content: Every other Monday, I arrive at work bleary-eyed, still finishing my coffee, and settle into the workweek by reviewing my latest pay stub. I’m looking for miscounted hours, abnormal deductions — the sorts of mistakes that never happen but could. This morning was different. I spent the weekend fixating on the sorry state of health insurance in this country, roused in large part by Democrats’ comprehensive midterm victory, including wins by supporters of Medicare for All like Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed. I arrived at my desk alert and reviewed my pay stub, focusing specifically on health care contributions. When we look at our pay stubs, employer and employee health insurance contributions combine into a number we numbly accept as we focus on our take-home pay. In my case, the biweekly total is $1,267. That adds up to about $33,000 over the year, higher than the average employer-sponsored family plan cost of $28,303 . Single-coverage plans average about $9,000, while workers buying on the marketplace pay upward of $7,500 annually ($12,000 in my home state of Alaska). These figures represent real, consequential lost wages. And they get higher every year. Health Insurance Premiums Are a Tax I have a stable union job with my local municipal government. My health insurance leaves a lot to be desired, often burdening my family with out-of-pocket costs (a reality brought home just last week during an emergency room visit for our daughter, who thankfully is fine). Still, it is better than what most American workers have. I am meant to feel lucky for it. Look at the alternatives: I could have a lesser plan with higher deductibles and out-of-pocket limits. I could have no insurance at all, like roughly 10 percent of Americans. Or scarier still, I could be forced to pay taxes into a single-payer system that removes health care from the workplace and covers everyone equally. But staring at a pay stub leaves us to wonder: What are health insurance premiums if not a tax? They’re compulsory; we can’t opt out. And even if we could, we would never expose ourselves to such catastrophic risk. The deduction is listed separately from federal taxes on the pay stub, but what makes it different? The answer is who gets the money. Our health care premiums are nothing other than a compulsory tax paid to private insurance companies instead of the federal government. When included with our other taxes, they make the United States one of the highest-taxed countries in the world — higher even than the Nordic states . The United States spends roughly 18 percent of its GDP on health care, double that of peer nations with universal health care systems. The oft-stated benefit of our system is that it saves us from taxes, but in fact it taxes us at a premium and sends the excess to insurers as profit. Worse, it burdens us with impossible out-of-pocket costs at our times of greatest need. Our paychecks suffer from this waste. Rising premiums help keep our wages stuck as employers weigh insurance and wages against the same bottom line. Every dollar diverted to surging premiums is a dollar stolen from our wages and benefits. All the while, workers shoulder ever-increasing deductibles and contribution shares. Your Paycheck Under Medicare for All You have heard, of course, that single-payer health insurance — Medicare for All — will cost trillions of dollars. It will raise your taxes. It will take away your hard-won and much-beloved employer-sponsored insurance. It’s tempting to argue the obvious: yes, Medicare for All will raise your taxes, but the increase in your taxes will be significantly lower than your current premiums and out-of-pocket costs, which will disappear. Looking at my pay stub, however, I don’t even want to concede that it will raise taxes. Again, payroll insurance contributions are a compulsory, unavoidable tax on your wages . Under Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All proposal, my employer (a budget-strapped municipal government) would pay $260 per paycheck through a 7.5 percent payroll tax, and I would pay $94 via a 4 percent income tax after standard deductions. The combined total of $354 represents $913 in savings — $23,738 over a year. Medicare for All will reconfigure your taxes, sure. But it won’t raise them. It will lower them. The $24,000 newly freed from my paycheck would land on the bargaining table in negotiations over my union’s next contract. Some of this will go directly to wage increases. Some will go to benefits. Some will stay with the municipal government. For all future negotiations, though, we will not have to tackle the albatross of rising insurance premiums. What Is Health Insurance For? Health care is expensive, costing trillions per year no matter who pays. Currently, it’s paid for in a convoluted, wasteful scheme: private insurers act as payers using funds taken from our wages, while the government covers its share in Medicare and Medicaid. The rest is paid out-of-pocket by patients in times of need. The effect is to chain us to our jobs, suppress our wages, and burden our negotiations. We all know this is not what health insurance is for. Health insurance is meant to minimize risk, minimize costs, and mitigate catastrophes. This can only be accomplished with a single, government payer. A true tax should fund a public good to benefit society, not drain your wages to benefit profiteers. With an overwhelming mandate and the policy still popular , Democrats ought to run a Medicare for All supporter in 2028 and make it their first priority in the new Congress. The policy will save up to a trillion dollars annually in overall spending. You can look at your pay stub to see where those savings will land. articles.title: RECAP: 2026 Member Mobilization Institute
articles.author: Joe Simpson
articles.content: RECAP: 2026 Member Mobilization Institute ONAWAY, MI – UAW members from across the country gathered at Black Lake for the 2026 Member Mobilization Institute, a week of learning new skills, sharing ideas, and exploring how we can strengthen our union together. Workshops, discussions, and hands-on practice challenged participants to consider what it takes to build lasting power and to prepare for the opportunities and challenges ahead, including May Day 2028. Learning continued beyond the classroom as delegates embraced opportunities to share their own worker stories by creating art with block printing, bandanas, signs, buttons, photography, and zines. Creativity became a powerful organizing tool, helping participants communicate their message, connect with others, and find their entry point in the movement. From inspiring art exhibits to a memorable evening that blended live music and labor history, delegates experienced firsthand how culture helps strengthen our collective action. Participants from across our nine regions, including Puerto Rico, formed new friendships and strengthened old connections, whether testing their knowledge at trivia, singing karaoke together, or joining a nature trail walk. As they return home, delegates carry fresh skills, new connections, and a renewed commitment to building active, engaged locals. The work ahead belongs to all of us, and this year’s Institute was a reminder that the strength of our union lives in the solidarity of its members and in what we’re determined to build together. articles.title: Jeffries Should Not Be Speaker
articles.author: Medea Benjamin
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Now that Democrats have swept the House, a key question is: Who should lead it? Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the first Black Speaker of the House, which would be a historic milestone. But members of Congress must examine Jeffries' record, his priorities, and the kind of leadership he would bring to this moment. Here are ten reasons why Jeffries should not be Speaker. 1. He has abandoned Medicare for All At a time when millions of Americans struggle with unaffordable health insurance, medical debt, and the threat of financial ruin from illness, Jeffries has distanced himself from one of the most important progressive reforms: Medicare for All. Jeffries co-sponsored Medicare for All legislation from 2013 through 2021. But in an August 2026 interview on NBC's Meet the Press , he said it is no longer legislation he supports or cosponsors. Ironically, he made that statement on the same day a CBS poll found that 90 percent of Democratic voters back the idea. This reversal puts him at odds with party voters, but also with a majority of Democratic representatives in the House. As of late October, Rep. Pramila Jayapal's Medicare for All Act had 118 Democratic cosponsors. A “leader” who won’t back what his own caucus and voters want is not a leader. 2. He refuses to break with Israel Perhaps nowhere is Jeffries more out of step with the progressive base than on Israel. For decades, Jeffries has been a staunch defender of the U.S.-Israel alliance. At a pro-Israel rally in 2014, during Israel's military assault on Gaza, Jeffries proclaimed, “Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever!.” In 2020 he told an AIPAC conference that New Yorkers consider Jerusalem their “sixth borough,” totally disregarding the plight of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation. Even as Israel's genocide in Gaza sparked worldwide outrage, Jeffries continued to resist calls to end U.S. military support. In July 2026, 103 House Democrats voted to cut $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel, including the party's second-ranking House leader, Katherine Clark. But Jeffries joined 97 other Democrats and nearly every Republican in voting to preserve the funding. In a May 2024 60 Minutes interview, when asked whether Israel's bombing of Gaza had been indiscriminate, Jeffries said no. By then, nearly 35,000 Palestinians had been killed. When the interviewer pressed him, saying, "You seem reluctant to criticize Israel at all," Jeffries responded, "I'm dealing with the facts on the ground." Related: Books or Bombs? French Students Protest Education Cuts as Military Spending Rises Jeffries has also refused to cosponsor the Block the Bombs Act, which would restrict transfers of some of the deadliest offensive weapons to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs, bunker busters, precision-guidance kits, and tank and artillery rounds. As of November 2026, the bill has 82 Democratic cosponsors and the endorsement of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Caucus Chair Greg Casar has pledged to push for a floor vote if Democrats regain the majority. Yet Jeffries has not signed on, and as Speaker, he would have enormous power to determine whether the bill ever receives a vote. While Jeffries has acknowledged that U.S. policy toward Israel needs to change, he continues to support Israel's military superiority and joint missile-defense programs. He has also refused to condemn Section 219 of the NDAA, which would further integrate U.S. and Israeli military research, technology, and production. Ironically, both Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu have recently suggested that the U.S. should stop giving Israel nearly $4 billion a year because “Israel doesn't need it.” Whether or not we believe them, it is striking that we have yet to hear a similar call from Hakeem Jeffries. 3. He has failed to champion major cuts to the obscene Pentagon budget At a time when Americans are struggling to afford basic necessities, Trump is demanding a staggering $1.5 trillion military budget—an increase of nearly $600 billion, or 66 percent, over the previous year's base funding. Yet Jeffries has not made substantially reducing Pentagon spending a central priority of Democratic leadership. Yes, he has opposed funding for Trump's war in Iran but he is a staunch advocate of continued U.S. military aid to Ukraine and has sharply criticized Trump for failing to provide sufficient support. He said “America is stronger when Russia is weaker.” In September 2026, he pledged that Democrats would continue backing Ukraine “until victory is won,” signaling his commitment to greater U.S. involvement and military assistance instead of a commitment to a diplomatic solution that would end that terrible war. Jeffries is also an enthusiastic defender of the aggressive alliance NATO, which should have dissolved when the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991. He has called NATO “the most successful military and diplomatic alliance in the history of the world.” NATO, at Trump’s insistence, has called for all members to dramatically increase their military budgets to 5 percent of their GDP (the US is presently at 3.1 percent). Jeffries’ ties to the military-industrial complex are particularly troubling. During the 2026 election cycle alone, Jeffries' campaign reportedly received approximately $212,000 from military PACs. Democrats cannot simply promise better healthcare, affordable housing, quality education and climate action while supporting a massive military budget. Real change requires shifting resources from weapons and war to the needs of ordinary people. The next Democratic Speaker must be prepared to challenge the military-industrial complex. 4. He continues to accept pro-Israel lobby money Jeffries's position on Israel cannot be separated from his longstanding political relationship with the AIPAC lobby. At a time when AIPAC funding has become toxic and so many Democratic candidates rejected AIPAC money, Jeffries has maintained his ties to the organization. According to Track AIPAC, Hakeem Jeffries has received more than $1.5 million in campaign contributions from AIPAC and other pro-Israel lobby groups over his congressional career. During the 2026 election cycle alone, his campaign received nearly $300,000 in contributions from pro-Israel PACs.He has also taken five AIPAC-sponsored trips to Israel since arriving in Congress. Following the November elections, AIPAC publicly celebrated Jeffries as one of the candidates it supported. How can congressional Democrats be led by someone so closely tied to AIPAC, a lobby increasingly toxic to their own voters? 5. His Backroom Dealings with Jared Kushner Raise Serious Questions About His Judgment At a time when Americans are demanding investigations into the Trump family's financial dealings, Hakeem Jeffries chose to sit down privately with Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and influential adviser. In August 2026, reports revealed that Jeffries had met with Kushner to discuss possible cooperation on housing, immigration and affordability. Yet Kushner, who holds no official government position, continues to wield influence over U.S. foreign policy while maintaining lucrative financial relationships with Gulf governments through his investment firm. House Judiciary Committee Democrat Jamie Raskin has already launched an investigation into Kushner's foreign financial entanglements, demanding documents and communications about his dealings with foreign governments. So why was Jeffries meeting with him behind closed doors? With Democrats taking control of the House in January, they need a speaker committed to untangling the dirty web of corruption committed by Trump and his inner circle. Related: The Urgency of Recognizing the Ansar Allah Government in Yemen 6. He Has Elevated Warhawks to Key Foreign-Policy Positions You can tell a political leader's priorities by whom they put in power. And Jeffries's choices speak volumes. In August 2026, Democratic leaders elevated Rep. Jared Moskowitz, one of the House's most outspoken pro-Israel hawks, to the top Democratic position on the powerful House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa. Moskowitz has been an unwavering defender of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, continued U.S. weapons shipments, and Israel’s brutal military operations in Lebanon. He has also openly supported both Israeli attacks on Iran and Trump's 2025 bombing of Iranian nuclear facilities, and initially opposed congressional efforts to prevent the 2026 war before later backing War Powers restrictions. With Democrats in control of the House, Moskowitz will be positioned to chair the Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee, wielding significant influence over congressional oversight and policy toward Israel, Palestine, Iran, and the entire region. Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Wesley Bell, two other staunch defenders of Israel, were added to the Foreign Affairs Committee. Bell had defeated progressive Rep. Cori Bush in 2024 after massive spending by AIPAC's super PAC. Progressives are still steaming over the role of Wasserman Schultz in undermining Bernie Sanders during the 2016 Democratic presidential primary. The backlash to these appointments was immediate. Rep. Ro Khanna warned, "Don't put Israel hawks out of touch with our voters in charge of our Middle East policy." The Council on American-Islamic Relations condemned the appointments as an insult to voters and an attempt to shield Israel from accountability for its actions in Gaza. 7. Jeffries Represents the Democratic Party's Dependence on Corporate Money The Democratic Party claims to fight for working people, but Jeffries remains deeply connected to the wealthy corporate interests that dominate Washington. His campaign has benefited from millions of dollars in contributions associated with Wall Street, pharmaceutical and insurance companies, real estate interests, Big Tech and military contractors. These financial relationships raise a fundamental question: How aggressively will Democrats challenge corporate greed, Wall Street speculation, soaring healthcare costs and the military-industrial complex when their leader maintains such close ties to these powerful interests? Progressive Democrats have demonstrated that grassroots organizing and small-dollar fundraising offer an alternative to corporate PAC money. The Democratic Party cannot credibly promise to take on corporate power without confronting the influence of big money within its own leadership. Related: Stop the War Machine: Start Rebuilding America 8. He has defended the Democratic establishment against progressive challengers Jeffries has a long history of protecting entrenched Democratic incumbents against progressive challengers. In 2020, he backed longtime pro-Israel congressman Eliot Engel against Jamaal Bowman, who defeated Engel in a stunning primary upset. In 2022, Jeffries traveled to Chicago to campaign for veteran Congressman Danny Davis against young progressive organizer Kina Collins, who came within seven percentage points of victory. And in 2026, Jeffries backed Dan Goldman, Adriano Espaillat and Shri Thanedar against progressive challengers Brad Lander, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Donavan McKinney. All three incumbents lost their primaries, and all three challengers went on to win in November. This pattern is no coincidence. In 2021, Jeffries joined forces with centrist Democrats Josh Gottheimer and Terri Sewell to establish Team Blue PAC, designed to protect Democratic incumbents against primary challengers. While voters are demanding a new direction, Jeffries has repeatedly sided with the establishment candidates they rejected. 9. He Wants to Reform ICE, Not Abolish It As ICE agents terrorize immigrant communities, separate families and carry out violent raids, the question of how to dismantle Trump's cruel mass-deportation machinery has become increasingly urgent. Jeffries has condemned ICE's brutality and demanded greater accountability. But he has stopped short of calling for the abolition of ICE or the dismantling of the Department of Homeland Security, insisting instead that these agencies can be reformed. Contrast that with Rep. Delia Ramirez's groundbreaking Reimagining Safety Act, which would abolish ICE, dismantle DHS and establish a new Department of Community Safety, redirecting resources toward housing, healthcare and community well-being. Her legislation challenges the very definition of national security, arguing that real safety comes from meeting people's needs, not militarizing their communities. This is the kind of bold, visionary leadership that offers a fundamental alternative to simply “reforming” an out-of-control immigration enforcement system that is terrorizing immigrant communities. 10. He Has Failed to Champion Bold Climate Action As devastating wildfires consume entire communities, record-breaking heat waves threaten lives, and floods and droughts wreak havoc across the country, the climate crisis demands bold, urgent leadership—not business as usual. Yet Jeffries has refused to endorse the Green New Deal or champion demands to halt the expansion of fossil fuel infrastructure and eliminate taxpayer subsidies to the oil and gas industry. In 2022, when more than 70 House Democrats publicly opposed legislation to fast-track fossil fuel projects, Jeffries declined to join them. More recently, he has distanced himself from calls for a moratorium on new AI data centers, even as a powerful grassroots movement is sweeping the country, with communities organizing against these energy-guzzling facilities that drain water supplies, drive up electricity bills, strain power grids and threaten the environment. Jeffries supported the Inflation Reduction Act's clean-energy investments, but he has not embraced the more ambitious climate agenda advocated by progressive lawmakers and community groups. At a time when climate disasters are destroying homes, livelihoods and entire communities, the Democratic Party needs leadership with the urgency and ambition to confront the climate crisis. Related: Why America’s Trillion-Dollar War Machine Is Failing in Iran A Democratic Majority Deserves Progressive Leadership More than any single vote, contribution, or appointment, the problem with Hakeem Jeffries is the establishment politics he represents—politics that protect the powerful, accommodate corporate interests, and offer timid reforms when the country is crying out for transformative change. Voters did not reject Republican extremism just to see Democratic leaders continue pouring billions into wars and corporate interests while families struggle to afford housing, healthcare, and basic necessities. And the grassroots are making their voices heard. In just a few days, more than one million people have signed a petition demanding new leadership. Congressional offices are being inundated with calls, and several incoming Democrats—including Melat Kiros, Claire Valdez, Chris Rabb, and Adam Hamawy—are withholding support for Jeffries. The Speaker of the House holds enormous power. That power can be used to confront the military-industrial complex, challenge corporate money and AIPAC, stand up for immigrants, and put human needs ahead of endless wars. Or it can be used to protect the very system that has brought us to this crisis. That’s why we need a new generation of leadership willing to fight for real change. Sign the petition demanding new leadership . Call your member of Congress at 202-224-3121.

articles.title: Impeachment Could Become A Powerful Tool
articles.author: Paul deLespinasse
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Some Democrats are threatening to impeach Donald Trump again in January when they have the majority in the House and Senate But enough Republicans will remain to block conviction since they will constitute more than one third of the Senate. Perhaps the third time would be the charm, since some Republican politicians are distancing themselves from him. But a successful impeachment probably needs to be led by Republicans. If initiated by Democrats, many Republicans would argue that the impeachment is just another partisan attack. However Democrats should not abandon all thoughts of impeachment. Rather than impeaching Donald Trump, however, they should impeach his more outrageous subordinates beginning with Pete Hegseth, Todd Blanche, Russell Vought, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Regrettably, Stephen Miller--- Trump’s new chief of staff--- is not considered a “civil officer” of the U.S. and therefore probably cannot be impeached. Representative Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) may introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth this week, and it may well pass the House even before Democrats have taken over because many Republicans can’t stand him. A president’s associates, as we will see, are more likely to be convicted by the required two-thirds Senate majority than he is. My Ph.D. dissertation examined the role of the king or queen in six constitutional monarchies. The history of Great Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark indicates that removing a leader’s subordinates can be a powerful way to control what that hereditary leader is doing. Related: One Sided View of Preposterous Lawsuit At PBS The old idea that “the king can do no wrong” persists in these countries despite the fact that they are democracies. These apparently conflicting facts are reconciled by requiring that royal decisions must have the “countersignature” of a minister who can be held accountable and ousted by the parliament. These countries thereby enjoy a strict separation of two roles. The monarch is ceremonial head of state. The prime minister is head of government. The monarch is theoretically all-powerful, but actual decisions are made by the cabinet under the leadership of the prime minister. The American presidency combines the two roles--- head of state and head of government--- in a single official. But like constitutional monarchs, the president, acting individually, has little actual power. Presidential decisions will have no real consequences unless they are carried out by subordinates--- cabinet members and the other people employed by their various departments. The analogy with the European monarchies, like all analogies, is not an exact one. In the United States, cabinet members are not picked by Congress and cannot be members of Congress. But thanks to the impeachment power set forth in the Constitution, cabinet members can be removed by Congress. And the Senate can block replacements put forward by the president. Our federal Constitution has no provisions for recalling the president. To the extent that American presidents are politically immune from removal by impeachment, they are therefore much like the unelected European monarchs. But the same limitation does not apply to impeachment of that president’s advisors and staff. Related: A Major Political Question: To Whom Did God Give Land? It will be easier to convince two-thirds of the Senate to convict mere presidential advisors than to convict the president. Impeachment supporters from the president’s party can argue that their loyalty to the president is firm but that the advisor has been giving the president bad advice. It would therefore be harder for a president to threaten to “primary” senators who, professing support for him, simply vote to remove the advisor. Removing an advisor would give the president both a motive and a face-saving way to reverse policies that the removed official had been administering. Although Harry Truman’s desk sign that “the buck stops here” would remain true, the advisor could be the scapegoat for problems that really were the president’s responsibility. And critics of the policy should be happy to see it reversed, even if the ultimately guilty president remains in office. Impeaching presidential advisors could become an important part of American government despite its repeated failure to remove presidents. It would strengthen the hand of Congress, today a weakened body despite the intent of those who wrote the Constitution to make it the strongest branch of government. It is not impossible for a president’s party to turn on him, as Richard Nixon found out. But the future importance of impeachment may lie mainly in its use to remove presidential advisors and, hopefully, reverse policies with which they have been associated.

articles.title: California UFCW Leaders Really Don’t Want Union Elections
articles.author: Lisa Xu
articles.content: In a union that has been headed by one family with no competitive elections since 1984, a group of grocery workers is organizing for change. But last week, they say, union staff who back the incumbent administration went to outrageous lengths in an attempt to make sure there’s no election this year either. On the afternoon of Monday, November 2, Eric Marcuz, a veteran Northern California Safeway worker, stopped at the union office to pick up blank petitions to get on the ballot in the union’s upcoming election. Marcuz is running for president on the At What Cost slate in the 23,000-member United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8–Golden State (8-GS), one of the largest locals in the union. To get on the ballot, Marcuz and his slate-mates have to collect 443 petition signatures — 2 percent of the local’s active members — by mid-November. If they don’t get enough signatures, no election will be held. After Marcuz picked up the petitions from the local’s Roseville office, he got in his car to drive three hours south to Fresno, to start collecting signatures with another candidate on his slate at a Save Mart store there. (The local spans a ten-hour stretch from Bakersfield up to the Oregon border.) When Marcuz stopped for gas, he said he noticed that a black Dodge Ram pickup stopped as well. When he got back on the freeway, so did the truck. At the next gas stop, Marcuz spoke to the man driving the truck. It was Jeff Berns, a staff representative for Local 8-GS. His brother, Mark, is also on staff at the union — and the local’s election chair, responsible for overseeing the election. Marcuz asked Jeff Berns why he was following him. According to Marcuz, Berns said he wanted to make sure that all the members got the “accurate information” that Marcuz’s slate was going to “divide” the union. He said he was going to follow him the entire time Marcuz was out, all the way back to Marcuz’s house in Redding, several hours north. Marcuz jokingly asked him if he needed a place to stay. Berns said he didn’t — because he’d been staying a lot in the Redding area lately himself, which Marcuz said he thought was “creepy” because that’s where Marcuz lives with his family (and is not where Berns lives). Berns would live up to his promise — following Marcuz for the next three hundred miles, through every stop, exit, and U-turn. He even followed him inside the Fresno Save Mart and camped out for an hour with another union rep while Marcuz ate dinner at a supporter’s house one hundred miles north in Modesto. No Competitive Elections At the gas station, Berns repeated the mantra, “Solidarity works!” That’s the motto of the incumbent president, Jacques Loveall, who is heading the Solidarity Works Team slate in this election. Loveall was appointed to lead the union in 2004, when his father, Jack Loveall, stepped down. The elder Loveall had held the top office since 1984; when he retired he was one of the highest-paid union officers in the country, earning the equivalent of $1 million today. (The Contra Costa Times reported that he had a $28,000-a-year country club membership and “two pilots on staff to chauffeur him in a private jet.”) Neither father nor son has ever faced a competitive election in the local. Back on the freeway, Marcuz called a Department of Labor agent whom he had already been in touch with. They had previously spoken about the local’s apparent attempt to cancel the election by merging with a mysterious organization called the Staffing Agencies Federated Employees, an entity that listed one of Loveall’s relatives as its president on its initial filing. The agent told him to report the intimidation to the election chair and tell him to get the rep to back off. Marcuz then called Mark Berns, the election chair, who he said told him he would talk to staff about acting in a professional manner. More Reps However, when Marcuz arrived at the Save Mart store in Fresno to begin collecting petition signatures, he and another slatemate, Mike Romero, said that three union reps were waiting for them, including Jeff Berns. One of the others was John Micheletti, a longtime Local 8 vice president. Far from being called off, they said, the intimidation had actually intensified. Marcuz and Romero said the reps interfered with every conversation they attempted to have with workers about signing their nomination petition. The very first worker they engaged about signing, a longtime acquaintance of Romero’s, fled once a rep entered the conversation and became confrontational. The worker did not sign the petition. “They were everywhere inside the store,” said Marcuz. At least one of the interactions was filmed on a phone. Marcuz said that Berns told him, “I’m going to make sure everyone knows who you are and not to sign that.” And additionally, “We’re going to invalidate every single signature that you get.” It is illegal for union staff and officers to campaign on union time. Berns said he was on vacation. Romero, who has worked at Save Mart for thirty years, said, “This is the most I’ve seen of union staff in six months.” He said a fourth rep turned up after Marcuz left. Seen This Before These tactics — following opposition candidates and invalidating signatures — have both been alleged by previous members of the local who attempted to challenge the Lovealls. A Contra Costa Times article published in 2004 reported that supporters of Loveall’s father got members to rescind their signatures to keep dissident candidate Jack Nordby off the ballot in 1997. A book written by then Local 588 reform activist Doug Slaydon states that as many as 150 signatures were removed. (Local 588 merged with another local to form Local 8-GS in 2006 — postponing a potential competitive election that year.) Nordby also alleged that he was tailed by a pickup truck while collecting ballot signatures, followed around by union reps in stores, and once chased in his car while driving his wife and two daughters to church. The Contra Costa Times also reported allegations that Local 588 staffers staked out the home of a member of UFCW Local 1179 who had led a successful rank-and-file opposition campaign to an attempted merger of the two locals and “tailed him in union cars.” “In June 1994,” reported the Times , the member, Michael Ross-Smith, “was rear-ended in Walnut Creek by three UFCW 588 business agents following him too closely in a white 1993 Ford Thunderbird leased to the union, according to a traffic collision report from the Walnut Creek police department.” Tailed for Seven Hours Marcuz and Romero said they quickly realized that they wouldn’t be able to collect petition signatures with this level of interference. Marcuz’s next stop was going to be to drop off petition forms with a supporter at the Turlock Safeway, over an hour to the north, but he made plans to meet the supporter at their house in Modesto instead. When Marcuz left the parking lot of the Fresno store, Romero said three vehicles followed him. Romero also realized that one of the reps had stayed behind, and he became worried that he would be followed as well. He drove around for a long time before going home, to make sure he wasn’t followed. Marcuz, meanwhile, said that Berns and Micheletti followed him for ninety miles, all the way to Modesto. They stayed parked outside the house while Marcuz ate burritos with the supporter — finally leaving after an hour, after 8 p.m. “It’s crazy that they would literally go two hours out of their way to make sure nobody else can talk to the employees,” Romero said. Marcuz said he almost canceled his plans to stay alone in a hotel in Roseville overnight, worried he would be tailed there, and contemplated driving for four more hours home to Redding. In total, he estimates he was followed for seven hours, over a distance of three hundred miles. Scare Tactics Section 610 of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act (LMRDA) forbids the threat or use of force or violence to restrain, coerce, or intimidate union members from exercising their right to nominate candidates or to vote in union officer elections, while Section 401(e) bars “improper interference” in the rights of union members to run for and support candidates for local union office. “It makes me think of everyone that has known there’s been a need for change in the past and has been scared away from pursuing it,” Marcuz said. While Marcuz and his slate are standing strong, he said, “this might work. They might intimidate and scare enough people out of participating.” In the morning, Marcuz filed a police report with the Roseville Police Department alleging stalking and harassment, citing the time and distance he was followed and the behavior he encountered in the Fresno store. Local 8 did not respond to requests for comment. Petition signatures are due November 17, and ballots will be mailed November 21. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
