articles.title: Youth in Revolt
articles.author: Henry A. Giroux
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Young people are taking to the streets across France, Italy, Belgium, India, Serbia, and Albania, refusing to surrender their futures to a capitalist system that has abandoned them or to a politics that Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor have described as “end times fascism.” These protests are fueled by mounting anger over deteriorating schools, economic insecurity, unaffordable housing, political corruption, and a ruling class increasingly indifferent to the needs and voices of the young. As far right governments in Europe, the United States, and Latin America cancel out a future plagued by endless wars, climate catastrophe, staggering inequality, deepening poverty, and deteriorating public institutions, young people are rethinking the language of politics, resistance, and hope. A 21-year-old student protesting in Milan captured this spirit of resistance in an interview with Reuters , declaring: “It’s vital to take part in people’s spontaneous movements born from an explosion of rage that made collective action possible.” She added, “I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream.” Rather than address these grievances, governments have increasingly responded with curfews, protest bans , and brutal police repression, treating the democratic aspirations of young people as threats to be crushed rather than demands for justice to be heard. These uprisings are driven by more than economic grievances. They express a growing refusal to accept the moral and political cruelty of a system that has declared the young disposable. At their core is a recognition that neoliberal capitalism has robbed an entire generation of the promise of a better future and that austerity is class warfare disguised as economic necessity. As reported in Rolling Stone , Mathys Le Coz Ndzié, a 17-year-old Parisian student, noted: “The current government hasn’t managed to give us a clear picture of the future, or the world we’re heading into. So we feel completely lost. … We haven’t been prepared for the world that’s coming. The one they’ve prepared us for no longer exists.” This war on youth is intensified by the destruction of social protections and the rise of governments that increasingly rely on surveillance, criminalization, and police repression to enforce obedience, especially among the poor and racially marginalized. Related: An Electoral Victory Is Not Liberation: The Fight Against Gangster Capitalism Yet out of these conditions of abandonment and repression, something more profound is emerging: a moral and political awakening rooted in the struggle for economic justice and a collective refusal to accept a world in which human dignity is sacrificed to private profit, democracy is hollowed out, and the very possibility of imagining and creating a different future is stolen from an entire generation. Carlotta Magoga , writing in European Democracy Hub, is right in stating that, “From Serbia to Bangladesh and Senegal, young people are becoming a driving force for a more democratic world. … In search of alternative routes, they are developing new forms of civic engagement — through artistic protest, online campaigns and storytelling — and rewriting the rules of political participation.” Through their courageous presence in the streets, they are fashioning a form of activism “as a way to rethink how democracy works.” For example, in France, students have challenged overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and a university admissions system that reinforces class inequality. In Italy, students have joined workers in protests over low wages, unaffordable housing , deteriorating public services, and increased military spending. In Genoa, port workers and students have also protested the use of ports for arms shipments . In Serbia, where opposition to government corruption has been central, students have demanded investigations into public contracts, government spending, and the political control of public institutions. These movements do not all embrace an explicitly anti-capitalist agenda, but their demands expose conflicts over who controls public resources, whose interests governments serve, and how economic and political power is organized and maintained. Capitalism, in one of its more disingenuous moments, celebrates youth rhetorically as the future but denies youth the resources to have a future. What governments fear about these revolts is that students are moving beyond demands to make capitalism more humane. Protests across Europe and beyond are challenging gangster capitalism as a political order marked by corruption, neoliberal austerity, authoritarianism, militarism, racism, and the concentration of wealth and political power in the hands of a financial elite. At the heart of this confrontation is a struggle over the moral and political values that will govern society and determine the fate of future generations. Two radically opposed moral visions are confronting one another on the world stage. One is rooted in solidarity, justice, and democratic possibility; the other in greed, racial hatred, organized brutality, and authoritarian domination. What is at stake is the future of democracy and whether coming generations will inherit a world governed by human dignity or one surrendered to the cruelty of the powerful. This culture of moral depravity finds one of its most revealing expressions in the U.S. billionaire class, where technological achievement is increasingly invoked to excuse political and moral cruelty. In an October 20 article in The Dispatch , Marian L. Tupy asks: “Is Elon Musk Worth the Trouble?” His defense of Musk turns technological achievement into a moral alibi for authoritarian politics, reducing the suffering produced by the exercise of billionaire power to an unfortunate price of technological progress. Missing from this calculus is any serious reckoning with Musk’s role in dismantling USAID , an assault on humanitarian assistance associated with catastrophic human suffering and potentially hundreds of thousands of deaths. Tupy’s invocation of Henry Ford is equally revealing. Ford’s antisemitism is reduced to an unfortunate character flaw, conveniently excused in the gratuitous celebration of industrial progress. This is the poisonous morality of gangster capitalism: technological progress divorced from justice, human suffering reduced to an acceptable cost, and billionaires shielded from moral accountability. The victims disappear while their powerful tormentors are celebrated. This is the moral rot of a political and economic order inhabited by the living dead, a world in which wealth and power can shield predators from accountability. The crimes of Jeffrey Epstein , who preyed on and trafficked underage girls for sexual exploitation, offer a chilling illustration of this culture of impunity. In this world of rapacious political zombies, wealth becomes a shield against accountability, and the victims of predatory power are condemned to silence. Related: France’s Student Uprising: A Generation Revolts Against Capitalism This culture of cruelty and unapologetic viciousness also reaches into electoral politics. Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign released an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, physician Amy Acton , denouncing her daughter as a liar. Acton has publicly described being removed from her mother’s custody at age 12 following sexual abuse by her stepfather. Her mother reportedly remained married to the accused man. Ramaswamy’s weaponization of Acton’s childhood suffering for political advantage reveals a political culture in which private trauma becomes electoral ammunition and cruelty becomes a badge of political power. This politics of dehumanization is also evident in the racist rhetoric surrounding the November elections. At a campaign event in Michigan, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. declared : “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce — they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Field prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize. They don’t produce literature.” These examples are not isolated instances. They expose a political culture and pedagogical regime organized around fear, racial hatred, and the degradation of human life. The language of social justice and compassion is increasingly displaced by the discourse of fascist cruelty, in which conscience is treated as weakness, domination becomes the measure of political power, and human suffering is transformed into a public spectacle. This is how a culture of cruelty becomes the pedagogical foundation of authoritarian rule. Against this culture of organized cruelty, young people are taking to the streets, transforming their anger into a collective struggle against the economic and political forces that have stolen their futures.Youth are rejecting the neoliberal fiction that individuals alone are responsible for their suffering. They are connecting private troubles to public injustices, building alliances with workers, teachers, and trade unions, and transforming anger into collective political agency. These struggles remind us that culture is not merely a reflection of politics — it is a central site of contestation where consciousness is formed, identities are shaped, and political possibilities are either destroyed or brought into being. Schools, media, digital platforms, and public institutions are powerful pedagogical forces. They can manufacture ignorance, obedience, and political indifference, or nurture the critical consciousness, historical memory, and collective agency essential to resisting authoritarian power. The United States cannot afford to regard these youth uprisings as distant spectacles. They offer a powerful indictment of the political and economic forces that are also destroying the foundations of U.S. democracy. Donald Trump’s response to the protests in France — referring to “people coming into the countries that hate the country” — reveals the fascist logic underlying his own war on youth, immigrants, and democratic dissent. Rather than acknowledge the legitimate grievances of young people protesting deteriorating schools, austerity, inequality, and the destruction of their futures, Trump has portrayed the unrest in France as the consequence of immigrants flooding Europe, claiming that France is being overrun by migrants who threaten Western civilization. This is the poisonous logic of fascist politics: erase the social conditions that produce resistance, transform the oppressed into enemies, replace demands for justice with racial hatred, and turn legitimate protest into a pretext for massive police repression. Under the Trump regime, the assault on public and higher education, the criminalization of dissent, the erosion of social protections, and the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a billionaire ruling class have become defining features of an increasingly fascist political order. Schools and universities are being transformed from institutions of critical inquiry and democratic possibility into laboratories of ideological conformity, corporate power, and political intimidation. Young people are being robbed not only of economic security but also of the public institutions, critical capacities, and collective hopes necessary to imagine a future beyond the brutality of gangster capitalism. What the United States needs is a generation unwilling to be schooled in obedience, stripped of historical memory, or taught to regard injustice as inevitable. It needs young people capable of challenging the machinery of authoritarian power and reclaiming education as a force for democratic resistance. Related: France’s Student Uprising: A Generation Revolts Against Capitalism The struggles unfolding across the globe offer a crucial lesson: Democracy cannot be defended through appeals to civility, symbolic gestures, or concessions designed to contain popular anger while leaving existing structures of power intact. It requires organized movements capable of uniting students, workers, educators, and communities in a sustained struggle for economic justice, human dignity, and democratic power. For too long, young people who have taken to the streets to challenge their political exclusion have been met with a mixture of admiration and condescension, celebrated for their idealism while their demands for fundamental change are dismissed, diluted, or met with brutal state repression. In France, this assault on dissent has taken an especially vicious turn. The French Senate has approved legislation dubbed the “Rioters Pay” bill , which could impose financial penalties of up to €10,000 on protesters, including those who did not personally cause property damage, while threatening to seize welfare benefits from impoverished families and parents of minors. This is both an attempt to crush dissent through financial intimidation and an act of state terrorism that threatens to turn poverty into an instrument of political repression, imposing devastating economic hardships on students and families already struggling under a punitive, austerity-driven neoliberal state. Rather than address the injustices driving young people into the streets, the government is seeking to make resistance itself a source of economic impoverishment. The irony here is particularly vicious. While the French government has met with student leaders and promised to meet several of their demands — including abolishing the controversial university admissions system, increasing funding for teachers, and investing in improvements to public schools — these promises have yet to be translated into concrete action. What has moved forward, however, is the machinery of repression. In fact, Amnesty International France condemned the French government for adopting “authoritarian practices [that seek] to silence dissenting voices by restricting space for expression.” Promises of educational reform remain unfulfilled, while the state moves with unrelenting speed to punish those who have taken to the streets demanding justice. Serbia offers a powerful rebuke to this politics of containment. Refusing to be pacified by cosmetic reforms, government reshuffling, or empty promises, student protesters transformed their outrage over corruption and authoritarian rule into a nationwide movement that ultimately defeated the ruling party of longtime right-wing leader Aleksandar Vučić in the October 25 election. Their victory demonstrates that young people need not settle for a place at the margins of a political system that has betrayed them. They can challenge the foundations of that system and turn collective resistance into a force capable of breaking the grip of entrenched power. Related: When Words Become Weapons of Racial Terror In France, too, student resistance has begun to yield results, forcing the government to promise to replace Parcoursup, the deeply unpopular university admissions platform, a limited but significant concession that demonstrates how collective struggle can compel those in power to retreat. India’s “Cockroach” movement over the summer has generated widespread unrest “ contesting the Hindu-nationalist movement” led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, suggesting “that he is vulnerable.” These struggles offer a lesson that extends far beyond Serbia, France, and India: Democracy has no future if the young are merely permitted to protest against the destruction of their futures, the brutality of austerity, and the systematic assault on their dignity and rights, while those responsible for these injustices remain securely in power. These uprisings are exposing a truth that neoliberal capitalism and its authoritarian defenders can no longer conceal: A system built on organized inequality, racial domination, dispossession, and the disposability of human life cannot be redeemed through cosmetic reforms or appeals to civility. Their struggle is not simply for a more humane capitalism, but against a system that has turned human life into a commodity, public goods into sources of private wealth, and democracy into a hollow ritual emptied of economic and political power. Frederick Douglass understood what is at stake when he declared: “If there is no struggle, there is no progress.” He added, “Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.” These young people are refusing the politics of resignation. They are insisting that a radical democracy must be fought for, that justice demands more than the redistribution of suffering, and that the future must be wrested from those who have made greed, violence, and domination the governing principles of society. Vuk Bačanović , writing about the Serbian student uprising, captures the spirit of resistance that now animates young people confronting authoritarian power across the globe. He writes: “At a time when democracy is retreating before the power of capital, authoritarian caprice, and a corrupt cynicism elevated to the status of statesmanlike wisdom, one generation has demonstrated that history has not ended, that obedience is not humanity’s destiny, and that no government is eternal.” Their revolt carries a message that ruling elites and authoritarian regimes can neither dismiss nor silence: The task is not to make the machinery of capitalist oppression more tolerable, but to dismantle it and struggle for a world in which justice, equality, and human dignity are not empty promises but the very foundations of democratic life. The challenge now is to transform these diverse uprisings into an international movement capable of sustaining their revolutionary energy, forging new forms of solidarity, and building the collective power necessary to bring an end to gangster capitalism and create a world in which democracy can breathe again. Truthout

articles.title: Vicious Racial Undertow
articles.author: Mark P. Fancher
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When the big blue wave came crashing through the most unlikely regions of the country, it washed ashore a remarkable group of newly elected racial, ethnic, gender and religious “firsts.” Progressives were of course gleeful. But if America’s history is any guide, joy about racial electoral breakthroughs may be premature. There is a well-established record of this country riding waves of legal and political progress toward the racial ideal, but at the same time being pulled backwards by a social undertow driven by white racists. There is no reason to believe things will be different after the recent mid-term elections. The push/pull racial dynamic has been here from the beginning. The abolition of slavery in 1865 was a step forward, but as formerly enslaved people began to make impressive political and economic gains during Reconstruction, the white community used terrorism to take the south backwards and to restore the old racial order. It was during that period that the Ku Klux Klan was established, and lynchings became community-wide celebrations. During the 20 th Century, the struggle against discrimination waged by the Civil Rights and Black Power Movements may have yielded civil rights legislation that moved the country forward, but many white voters took us backwards when they embraced Richard Nixon’s coded pledge to restore “law and order” which when translated meant the Black militants would be repressed and put back in their place of subjugation. Related: The Establishment’s Wild and Crazy Lies About Black Folks and Socialism In the 1970s, when the courts sought to move forward by enforcing the long-ignored 1954 Brown v. Board of Education school desegregation ruling with court-ordered busing, white parents responded with violent non-cooperation intended to take the country backwards. Also, affirmative action offered real potential for achieving racial equity in higher education, but the broad masses in the white community came to regard these programs as “reverse discrimination” and they successfully fought them in the courts, in legislatures and in the streets. In the 1980s, the movement for racial justice may have succeeded in having Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.’s birthday declared a national holiday, but at the same time the country embraced and revered Ronald Reagan and his ongoing efforts to gut civil rights legislation and undo much of what King accomplished. In the 1990s, Bill Clinton may have presented himself as a champion of racial justice, but he was shrewd enough to understand the racist sentiments of many in the white community, and he pandered to them, most notably in his attack on Sister Souljah. In 2008, many would have been willing to bet that the election of Barack Obama marked the dawn of a new day in this country, and some went so far as to proclaim the beginning of a “post-racial” era. However, the true sentiments of many in the white community were channeled into a racial undertow that dragged the country backwards when in 2016 they elected Donald Trump. So, as 2026 draws to a close, we find ourselves in the wake of the election of many racial “firsts,” and yet again there is widespread optimism that the country has found its way. But an inner voice informed by our history counsels otherwise. Because the tradition in this country is for white racism to drag racial progress backwards, we are compelled to go beyond the self-delusion enabled by conventional political pundits and to examine objectively the full measure of our collective experience over the past two years. Related: What’s Love Got to Do with Socialism? Most political analysts babble endlessly about voters’ collective sense of betrayal. The talking heads suggest that presumably, Trump received support in 2024 because of his promises to: abstain from endless wars, lower the cost of living, release the Epstein files, “drain the swamp,” and secure the borders. It is suggested that the mid-term results occurred because Trump failed to honor these pledges and the financial consequences hit his supporters hard. This analysis contains elements of truth, but it distorts and ignores hard, ugly facts about the persistent racist undertow that has always raged beneath the surface in this country. Trump’s support had little to do with his posture as a populist reformer. It had almost everything to do with his coded promise to conduct a race-oriented ideological pogrom and physical purge of non-white communities, and to then make real the idea of a “white nation.” He conducted a mean-spirited, hateful campaign grounded in and fueled by fear. It was a fear that this country’s white population is diminishing and its rates of growth are substantially outpaced by not only birth rates of resident communities of color, but also by immigrants from the southern hemisphere. In the minds of Trump’s supporters, to make America great again is to make America white again. When it is suggested that voters’ repudiation of Trump reflects a rejection of his fascist proclivities, that is true of only part of the electorate. We know this because his support remained steady throughout his first year in office. During that first year Trump was a very busy fellow, and among his highest priorities was the prosecution of his own little race war. He set out to eliminate federal DEI programs. He shut down FAA diversity hiring. He threatened to withhold federal research grants from universities that maintained race-oriented initiatives. He threatened private federal contractors that were not on board with his racial agenda. He declared his opposition to museums that he regards as offensive to white sensibilities. The National Museum of African American History and Culture was a special target. Public school districts were threatened with loss of Department of Education funding if they persisted with DEI programs. Trump was literally obsessed with race. With the blessing of the Supreme Court, ICE was greenlighted to use racial profiling during their round-ups. Although Trump railed endlessly against immigrants, he shamelessly encouraged the immigration of white people from non-“shithole countries.” He even went the extra mile to get white Afrikaners from South Africa to come to the U.S. to escape a mythical genocide. The military’s removal of memorials and memorabilia honoring heroic people of color was especially obnoxious. Through it all, the country cheered Trump on. It’s not simply that Trump’s overall approval ratings remained stable throughout this racist rampage. Pew Research Institute reported that in April of 2025, 44 percent – nearly half of the population – specifically approved of Trump’s DEI policies. Because that figure includes people of color and others with progressive racial views, it is likely that they are the only reason the approval rate was not higher. Among Republicans, 78 percent approved of Trump’s racist crusade against DEI. Related: Time for Reparations and a Do-Over of the Entire U.S. Project What then accounts for the mid-term election results? Did white people and people of color who sought white privilege by voting for Trump in 2024 have a racial epiphany? That’s unlikely. It’s more likely that they thoroughly appreciated the targeting of “illegals,” Blacks, Muslims, LGBTQ communities, and all of the “others” threatening prospects for a white America. But ultimately, when ICE killed two white people, and tariffs and war drove up the cost of fertilizer and diesel fuel for big rigs, and the lives of white people became otherwise miserable because of Trump’s policies, racists learned the hard way that, as Bob Marley said: “When the rain falls, it don’t fall on one man’s house.” So, in the end, was there a massive repudiation of Trump? Absolutely. But there was not a repudiation of his racism. There was a massive expression of anger that he had betrayed the cause of white nationalism with policies and practices that harmed white people. And it is likely that this hatred and anger will manifest in new and different ways as time passes, and many will wonder why people who rejected Trump will sink to new lows in matters concerning race. What then is to be done? It should be obvious that America does not have a problem that can be resolved in the political and legal arenas, because the dilemma concerns the people’s character and morality. Just as a swimmer caught in the undertow should not swim forward or backwards but should instead strike out in an entirely different direction, this country’s spiritual bankruptcy must be addressed in unusual ways. Much of the Democratic Party’s recent success is due to the willingness of many of their candidates to go in a different direction politically. Rather than writing off states believed to be irreversibly red, campaigns engaged Republican voters who, because of their personal pain, responded and voted blue. To effectively address this country’s racial intolerance, a similar approach is needed, but because the problem is spiritual it should not be dealt with as a political project. Although bigots harbor racist views, they nevertheless mistakenly regard themselves as moral. Their spirituality, such as it is, is often developed within white Christian nationalist settings and institutions which promote a warped, twisted, blasphemous theology that in many ways affirms white supremacy and the othering of fellow human beings. Consequently, in addition to challenging the politics of reactionary forces, there is a compelling need to challenge the theology of white Christian nationalism. That fight needs to be taken into white Christian nationalist churches where the stark contradictions between the tenets of white Christian nationalism and the Christian gospels can be highlighted, debated and heard by congregations. They need to be challenged to justify for themselves why they buy into a theology that regards the white community as God’s chosen people when Jesus himself was clearly a person of color who challenged his followers to love and embrace all people, including strangers from foreign lands and the poorest of the poor. How is it that they justify sitting in pompous judgment of others when Jesus specifically admonished his followers to not only leave all judgment to God, but to also embrace sinners in need of redemption and salvation? It’s of course likely that many who are challenged to reassess their commitment to white Christian nationalism will not listen and might even go on the attack. But we will never know whether a progressive racial message will resonate with at least some of these people unless an effort is made to engage them. If during those encounters they are touched by the Holy Spirit, anything can happen. After all, who would have ever believed that Scott Colom’s outreach to Mississippi MAGA folks would actually bear fruit?

articles.title: Reactionary Feminists Offer Bad Solutions to Real Problems
articles.author: Kaja Kröger
articles.content: To more and more people, the promises of sex-positive liberal feminism feel empty. The sexual ideas that have dominated feminism in the last two decades — including that sexual liberation always serves women’s interests, that consent is the only relevant sexual ethic, and that consuming porn and buying sex are benign practices like any other — are beginning to ring hollow. In this context, an emergent theoretical strand with the pointed, self-chosen name “reactionary feminism” has drawn considerable attention. It calls into question the liberal assertion that every form of sexual morality is anti-feminist — a view the Left has absorbed in recent decades. Although they work to maintain an appearance of ideological ambivalence, reactionary feminists are aligned with the post-liberal right , and they are finding success in attracting to that project women who are disenchanted with feminism’s wholesale embrace of sexual openness for its own sake. Their prescriptions are often at odds with what many feminists would consider emancipatory, but they are identifying real flaws in liberal feminism, and the Left should take notice. At the forefront of this new conservative feminism are British authors Mary Harrington and Louise Perry. Both have written popular books on how postwar sexual liberation in the West has failed women. In her 2022 book The Case Against the Sexual Revolution , Perry argues that shifting cultural norms around casual sex have led to a hookup culture that frustrates many women — even if they endorse these norms politically. In Perry’s telling, this is no wonder: as rigid sexual morality has receded, a liberal feminist paradigm has taken its place, one that de-exceptionalizes sex and portrays it as inconsequential. With contraception and a sexual culture in which casual sex doesn’t require emotional commitments, why would we need to have special guardrails around sex? For straight women on the dating market, this often manifests as feeling simultaneously sexually pursued and emotionally neglected. Many liberal women are responding to this dilemma with heteropessimism, or a bleak outlook on male-female pairings altogether. While reactionary feminism indulges its own form of gender fatalism (I return to this below), Perry is suggesting that these disappointed women look elsewhere: the problem is not heterosexuality but a culture of sexual casualness pursued erroneously in the name of progress. By making implicit liberal assumptions about casual sex and social progress explicit, Perry taps into intuitions most people share: for instance, that the expectation of emotional commitment after having sex is not too much to ask, or that sex can be a site of exceptional vulnerability and risk. Her willingness to say these things aloud has earned her an audience eager to hear something more nuanced than slogans about sexual autonomy. Frustration With Liberal Sexual Culture In academic feminism, sex is often presented as a banal activity, like going on a walk together. What happens in the course of sex is equivalent to deciding to go down this path or climb up this hill — with both people able to say at any time that they would like to turn around and go back home. This neutralized view of sex might appear emancipatory, promising as it does to overturn the sexual scripts and social stigmas that hold up the status quo. But unfortunately, it doesn’t align with actual experience. The vulnerability and boundary crossing involved in sex can have far-reaching consequences if someone takes advantage of them. For most people, the stakes of sex going well or poorly are thus much higher than those of going on a walk, even when people consider it casual. The broad Left’s consensus on this view of sex poses a dilemma for many women. If I’m expecting emotional engagement from a man after a hookup, does that secretly make me “trad” and a conservative? If monogamy fosters moralism and possessiveness in sexuality, does that not make nonmonogamy far more feminist? The success of Perry’s book, which came out when #MeToo was still relatively fresh, and there was cultural space to consider the potential downsides of sexual liberalism, suggested that many women had been privately entertaining these questions for years. Perry shined a light on the gap between political endorsement of goals like sexual freedom and conflicted attitudes about what that actually looks like in real life. There is no doubt that being “sexually liberated” — expressed, for instance, by engaging in nonmonogamy and kink or BDSM — has accrued social status and moral value among progressive feminists. Countless self-help books and articles about ethical nonmonogamy have come out in recent years. It seems simply cool to be chill enough to have an open relationship and not to really want someone to commit only to you. The alternative of wanting a committed romantic partner is, by contrast, conservative and uncool. Last year, writer Chanté Joseph went viral with a Vogue article that aptly captured this dynamic and asked, “Is having a boyfriend embarrassing now?” One of the women Joseph quotes says that having a boyfriend feels “Republican.” A hard blow for romantics. At the same time, it has also become cool to enjoy more physically violent sex. We can see this most evidently in the mainstreaming of “kinky sex” in popular culture since Fifty Shades of Grey . Data backs this up. If you’re a woman under twenty-four, the chance that your partner choked you during your last sexual encounter is about one in three, according to a representative survey by Indiana University researcher Debby Herbenick. Among millennial women (age twenty-five to thirty-nine), the figure was only 11 percent, and for women above the age of forty, it was 3 percent. This is an immense shift in sexual behavior across a single generation. In interviews with psychologist Nicola Gavey, young women who experienced such “rough sex” said they felt pressured by current sexual norms to make themselves want it in order not to seem boring or prudish. The reality of these parallel cultural developments is what makes Perry’s critique of liberal sexual culture more complicated than closed-minded conservative moralism. Marxist Rhetoric Reactionary feminists are not hesitant to offer women well-established conservative solutions for sexual liberalism’s discontents: refrain from casual sex, don’t get drunk with strange men around, get married. But they wrap these solutions in new leftist rhetoric. For many liberal and leftist feminists, marriage is a historically sexist institution aimed at controlling women and property. For Mary Harrington, by contrast, marriage enables “radical solidarity between the sexes.” It acts “as the smallest possible unit of resistance to overwhelming economic, cultural and political pressure to be lone atoms in a market,” as she writes in her 2023 book Feminism Against Progress . Rather than striving to be a girlboss or buying yourself flowers, Harrington proposes an attractive vision of monogamous marriage as radical solidarity. Who wants to be a lone atom in the market? In her book, Harrington argues that the belief in progress has led feminism astray: toward individual freedom, away from solidarity and care for others. For Harrington, this has to do with extending the concepts of freedom and trade from the economy to human relationships. But this “logic of individual profit” goes against our human nature as social animals. Harrington therefore wants to defend the relational interests of humans against “the market’s power to liquefy, to commodify and to alienate.” The concepts of commodification and alienation are laden with the Marxist critique that capitalism is not the right way to organize work and production. From a Marxist perspective, commodification and alienation are wrong because they thwart what is most distinctive about being human: free conscious activity (you could call that human nature). In the reactionary feminist view, things are not as clear. The cases of commodification they focus on are surrogacy, prostitution, and paying another woman to take care of one’s children. Reactionary feminists are quick to use leftist rhetoric in their critiques, but they remain vague about why surrogacy and prostitution are wrong. Is it because no one should divert women’s bodies from their “proper” use — reproductive sex within heterosexual marriage? Or is it because of the exceptional nature of exploitation involved in renting a woman’s womb or circumventing the mutuality of sexual attraction with money? We can find indications for both lines of argument in Harrington and Perry. Struggle of Interests For Perry, it is no wonder that men and women have had very different experiences in this liberated sexual culture. She argues that men and women have fundamentally opposing interests in the “sexual marketplace,” as she calls it, a contention that revolves around divergent proclivities and vulnerabilities rooted in biological reality. Women may be choosier about mates, for example, because women are uniquely vulnerable to becoming pregnant and bearing children after a sexual encounter, whereas men’s reproductive imperatives may motivate them toward sexual novelty and variety. For Perry, drawing on a concept that the Marxist radical feminist Shulamith Firestone first introduced, women thus constitute a “sex class,” which is locked in conflict with an opposing class, even while heterosexual men and women are oriented toward each other. If women and men simply have different interests by nature, then the possible political solutions seem reassuringly simple. One can become a revolutionary to overthrow nature (Firestone wanted to outsource pregnancy to artificial wombs) or become fatalistic about sexual relationships between men and women. While reactionary feminists tend to push back against heteropessimism, they are guilty of a version of it themselves. To them, women and men can never fully overcome their fundamental struggle of interests. We must all instead make peace with them and tame them through institutions like marriage, which they argue contains the excesses of an unchecked sexual marketplace. The problem with proclaiming an eternal struggle of interests between women and men is that it obscures the forces of socialization on gender relations and sexual violence. It takes women’s submission and men’s aggression to be natural facts. For Perry in particular, each notable difference in men and women’s behavior ultimately comes down to how women and men are simply wired differently and always have been. Although she is a critical thinker in other regards, Perry is captivated by evolutionary psychology and very keen to incorporate every “just-so” story that emanates from the field. Feminists have often disputed and criticized this science for naturalizing what is inherently social: gender roles. In the status quo, then, Perry might be right that women and men have different interests in the “sexual marketplace.” But when we take gender roles into account — and resist being satisfied by speculative stories that neatly explain how each gender stereotype has a deep root in our prehistory — we can begin to see that it needn’t be this way forever. Conservative Materialism With their Marxist rhetoric, reactionary feminists pick up, in a new and more explicit way, a well-established materialist thread in conservative argument: washing machines did more for the advancement of women than equal rights ever could. Conservative crusader Phyllis Schlafly declared as much in the 1970s. If we step back from the obvious political function of Schlafly’s assertion — cementing the view that homemaking is women’s true nature — we can see a materialist argument. Schlafly claims that what changed women’s lives and work most profoundly was not equal rights but electricity, mass food production, and household appliances. Harrington argues in a similar albeit more sophisticated vein that “the story of feminism is one of economic transitions — and particularly of the Industrial Revolution.” What enabled feminism’s fight for women’s equal rights was that women went from being producers in the agrarian household to wage workers and consumers. Harrington holds that as capitalism made work “more centralised, more mechanised and less agrarian, the resulting split between ‘work’ and ‘home’ drove women increasingly into a domestic-only role.” In the reactionary feminist view, then, the core of feminist politics is less a question of moral progress than of material conditions. This sounds eerily similar to a Marxist feminist perspective. And it also seems at odds with propagating women’s and men’s eternal struggle of interests. But Harrington and Perry see the biologistic opposition of interests as part of the material conditions of women’s lives. In doing so, they muddle the concerns of those radical feminists who are hyperfocused on women’s biology, with those of Marxist feminists, who look at economic and structural reasons for women’s situation. Reactionary feminists use ideological ambivalence as a strategy in their political project. As Harrington told The Atlantic about her book: “There are a great many conservatives who haven’t noticed quite how much Marxism I’ve smuggled in.” But she is also candid about the mission of reactionary feminists to build conservative and, if need be, “illiberal” institutions. Why the Left Should Care Reactionary feminists aim to convince us that, given the persistence of sexual violence and disrespect of women in liberal sexual culture, monogamous marriage is our best choice. They assert gendered behavior and preferences to be natural facts that we can only passively defer to — women and men will allegedly always have antagonistic interests due to their supposedly ingrained and static biological imperatives. Although they use Marxist rhetoric, their concept of women’s interests lacks a clear class analysis. While they acknowledge that not all women have the same interests, they never address class antagonism in capitalism but rather talk solely of the cultural expressions of “liberalism” and “market society.” That said, the Left needs to take seriously the offer reactionary feminists make to women dissatisfied with liberal feminism: a clear-cut judgment that what flies under the banner of sexual freedom is not always good for women. The rapidly rising number of women who are choked during sex, often enough against their will, is just one telling example of a sexual culture in which women still experience a lot of harm. This harm persists even though rigid sexual moralism has considerably lessened or fallen away. Adherents of sex-positive feminism have little to say about this — for fear of moralism — and understandably so. But that fear has created a void in which it is difficult to talk about what sex should and should not look like. A substantive feminist vision of sexuality and of what the good life for a woman is could fill this void. Instead, conservative women have mostly filled it with their gender fatalism. Many on the Left mistakenly think of all feminist cultural critiques as moralism that distracts from the real concern: economic interests. As the Russian revolutionary Alexandra Kollontai argued more than a century ago, even under socialism, people still need morality to guide gender relations and sexuality. Sexual violence does not disappear through economic reorganization. Thus women also have a material interest in something that is difficult to grasp in purely economic terms: comradely men. But the feminist left rarely taps into this moral critique. There seems to be a larger focus on poses of political radicalism (like abolishing the family) that can be hard to relate to for the majority of people. Reactionary feminists are right that it does women no favors when enjoying “rough sex” becomes a marker of being liberated. They are right that the sexual revolution’s promise of freedom has left many women feeling unsatisfied and vulnerable. But they are wrong in proclaiming women’s perpetual vulnerability for biological reasons. What they ignore is that women’s vulnerability is socially made and culturally scaffolded, and that there can be a society in which biological sex does not make women vulnerable. However, such a world requires not only a widely shared vision of gender equality but also the willingness to proclaim some sex practices as bad for those involved. Even if it’s a hard pill to swallow for those for whom feminist politics means radicalizing liberalism, such a world will require some degree of sexual morality. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: The Dollar’s Power Never Came From Oil
articles.author: Matías Vernengo
articles.content: The war in Iran and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have renewed an old debate about the foundations of American global power. Oil has been central to the geopolitical order dominated by the United States since World War II. The dollar is the principal international currency, oil is overwhelmingly priced in dollars, and American military power has been essential to controlling access to petroleum, particularly in the Middle East. The question raised by some analysts is whether the erosion of this arrangement, accelerated by the transition to cleaner sources of energy, signals the end of American hegemony and of the privileged position of the dollar. There are good reasons to take this possibility seriously. China has become the leading producer of solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles, and many of the technologies essential to the transition away from fossil fuels. The transition to new energy technologies could therefore profoundly reshape the distribution of global economic power at a time when American military superiority is being questioned. But there is a problem with moving directly from the decline of petroleum to the decline of the dollar. International monetary hegemony does not depend primarily on which commodities are traded, and only secondarily on which country possesses technological superiority in the industries of the future. It rests on a broader structure of fiscal, financial, productive, and military power that has historically developed over centuries. Understanding that distinction requires looking beyond oil to the historical relationship between money and empire. The Hydrocarbon Dollar Thesis An influential interpretation of international economic power emphasizes the relationship between energy technologies and geopolitical hegemony. Britain’s rise coincided with the coal-powered Industrial Revolution, while American dominance was associated with the age of petroleum, particularly as oil became essential to modern warfare and transportation. In this interpretation, China’s predominance in renewable energy technologies raises the possibility of another hegemonic transition. Daniel Bessner has suggested that China’s predominance in renewable energy technologies may herald that transition. Helen Thompson, in her book Disorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century , provides a sophisticated historical version of this argument. She shows how successive energy regimes shaped imperial rivalry, international finance, and the geopolitical conflicts of the twentieth century. For her, oil altered the material foundations of military and geopolitical power, creating a structural disadvantage for Britain and an advantage for the United States. Britain had become the leading industrial and naval power during the age of coal, a resource it possessed in abundance. The transition to oil, initially for naval propulsion and subsequently for motorized transportation and aviation, changed the strategic equation. In 1911, Winston Churchill, as First Lord of the Admiralty, decided that oil should replace coal in the Royal Navy. Oil-powered ships offered military advantages, but the change created a serious strategic vulnerability. The energy transition forced Britain to import a resource it previously did not need. In addition, the United States possessed an enormous advantage in oil production. Its rapidly expanding oil industry gave it the capacity to supply both its own economy and the Allied war effort. Thompson notes that approximately 80 percent of the oil used by the Allies in World War I came from the United States. During the interwar period, British governments tried to establish secure supplies through their Middle Eastern concessions. Nevertheless, their reliance on western hemisphere oil persisted. During World War II, Britain again needed oil supplied by American companies, paid for in dollars. Thompson’s point is not simply that oil was a superior energy technology. It is that the geographical distribution of petroleum reserves fundamentally altered the capacity of competing states to sustain modern warfare. More importantly, Thompson’s contrast between Britain’s ascent during the age of coal and America’s ascent during the age of oil suggests that, in the next renewable energy age, based on minerals, batteries, and electrification, China might become the key player. There is much to this argument. Countries that depend heavily on imported oil are vulnerable to changes in international oil prices and the availability of foreign exchange. The expansion of renewable energy can reduce these vulnerabilities. It may also weaken the strategic importance of oil-producing regions and the influence of countries that dominate them. But reducing the external dependence associated with energy imports is not the same thing as escaping the international monetary hierarchy. The ascent of the United States implied that the infrastructure of international trade and finance was organized around the dollar — most clearly after the Bretton Woods Agreement in 1944. Many internationally traded commodities, including oil, were priced in dollars. By the 1970s, after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system and the two oil shocks, oil-exporting countries earned large dollar surpluses and recycled their revenues through American banks and Treasury bonds. The petrodollar system thus helped sustain the international demand for the dollar. A conventional fear is that international investors might lose confidence in the dollar and shift their holdings into other assets. If the international demand for dollars is partly sustained by the hydrocarbon economy, then a transition to renewables could reduce that demand and thereby weaken dollar hegemony. In that sense, petrodollars might become eventually battery-renminbis. However, pricing oil in another currency would not necessarily undermine the international role of the dollar. Foreign exchange markets make it possible to acquire currencies for particular transactions without fundamentally changing the denomination of international debts, the composition of reserves, or the structure of international credit. The critical question is therefore not simply what currency is used to purchase oil, even if that matters. It is why the rest of the world continues to need dollars, and why the United States does not face a comparable need for foreign currencies. Money and the Fiscal-Military State Another explanation, developed recently by Ho-fung Hung in Greenback Empire , places geopolitical and military power at the center of international monetary relations. The postwar international monetary order was intrinsically connected to the overwhelming predominance of the United States following World War II. First its wartime allies, and subsequently even its former enemies, Germany and Japan, became dependent on American military protection.The United States also exercised considerable control over access to strategic commodities, particularly petroleum, and maintained close security relationships with major oil-producing countries, even as they sought greater autonomy through the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). Even geopolitical adversaries remained, to varying degrees, dependent on the dollar-centered international financial system. The widespread use of dollars and accumulation of American financial assets cannot be separated from these political and strategic relationships. The resulting system is self-reinforcing. American military superiority supports the international role of the dollar, while dollar hegemony allows the United States to sustain military expenditure and international commitments on a scale that would be considerably more difficult for other countries. Nevertheless, a fuller explanation requires placing these relationships in a longer historical perspective. The fiscal-military state was central to the development of modern capitalism and the rise of successive hegemonic powers. Public debt, central banking, and military expenditure did not merely support economic development after the fact. They were essential institutions in the creation of modern capitalist economies. The Bank of England, founded in 1694, was established principally to finance the British state during its wars against France. Public debt became the foundation of an expanding financial market. The central bank helped transform government obligations into liquid financial assets, supporting both private finance and state expenditure. The development of the British fiscal-military state, to use John Brewer’s apt concept, allowed the government to finance its navy, sustain prolonged wars, protect commercial routes, and promote the international expansion of British capitalism. This process helped establish the foundations of sterling’s international predominance. It was not simply that British industrial and naval power made sterling an international currency. The institutions associated with public finance and monetary development helped create that industrial and naval power in the first place. The same relationship would later emerge in the United States. Government expenditure, public credit, and the creation of financial institutions supported national economic integration and industrial development. Alexander Hamilton understood the significance of public debt and banking institutions for the construction of a national economy. The federal fiscal and monetary apparatus developed further during the Civil War, while the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913 helped establish the financial infrastructure required for the dollar’s international expansion. The relationship between fiscal-military and monetary power is circular. The fiscal capacity anchored in taxation, public debt, and central banking makes possible government expenditure on military procurement and research that promotes technological development and military power. These capabilities, together with geopolitical alliances and financial institutions, help sustain the international use of the hegemonic currency as the unit of account in trade and debt contracts, and as the main reserve asset. Monetary predominance then reinforces the original advantage. The hegemonic state can borrow and settle its external obligations in its own currency without having to accumulate foreign exchange as other countries do. It also acquires leverage over the external financial constraints faced by other states through its control over international liquidity and financial infrastructure. Rather than deriving simply from commodity pricing, market confidence, or network effects, monetary hegemony is thus both a product of fiscal-military power and a central means of reproducing it. How Britain Actually Lost Monetary Hegemony The transition from British to American hegemony provides a particularly revealing historical example of how currency competition works. It is tempting to associate Britain’s decline with the transition from coal to petroleum, just as it is tempting to interpret America’s current difficulties as a consequence of its attachment to fossil fuels. Energy certainly mattered. Coal was fundamental to British industrialization and naval power, while petroleum became increasingly important for modern transportation and warfare. But the crucial transformation in the international monetary hierarchy occurred through a different mechanism. During the nineteenth century, Britain was the world’s principal financial center. London supplied international credit, financed trade, and exported capital on an enormous scale. Sterling became the leading currency of international transactions. As Jay Sexton shows in Debtor Diplomacy , the United States, despite its growing productive capacity, remained dependent on British finance. American railroads, infrastructure, and industrial expansion benefited from access to London’s capital markets, which British financial diplomacy helped facilitate. By the beginning of the twentieth century, however, the United States had become the world’s largest industrial economy. Its productive predominance was not yet matched by equivalent international monetary power. World War I transformed this relationship. Britain entered the war as the leading international creditor but became increasingly dependent on American productive resources and finance. Maintaining its military commitments required massive purchases from the United States, financed through the liquidation of foreign assets and increasingly through American credit. By 1917, Britain could no longer sustain its war effort without substantial American financial assistance. The United States, which had previously depended on British finance, emerged from the war as the principal international creditor. John Maynard Keynes, who worked at the British Treasury dealing with the interallied web of debts, observed that “[i]n another year’s time we shall have forfeited the claim we had staked out in the New World and in exchange this country will be mortgaged to America.” The transformation of monetary power followed. The creation of the Federal Reserve supported the development of dollar-denominated trade finance. As suggested in Charles Kindleberger’s classic account of the interwar period, The World in Depression, 1929 – 1939 , the economic collapse and the geopolitical turbulence that led to two world wars were intrinsically connected to the global crisis of British hegemony and the absence of a clear hegemonic power. World War II and the establishment of the Bretton Woods system institutionalized American monetary predominance. Sterling continued to play an important international role, particularly within the sterling area, but Britain had become subordinate to the United States. As David James Gill shows in The Long Shadow of Default , American financial assistance through Lend-Lease, the 1946 Anglo-American Loan, and Marshall Plan aid had cushioned Britain’s decline. At Suez, Washington demonstrated that it could also use its financial predominance to impose constraints. The Suez Crisis of 1956 dramatically demonstrated the limits of American support. When Britain and France, together with Israel, intervened militarily against Egypt following the nationalization of the Suez Canal, the Eisenhower administration opposed their operation. Britain faced a financial crisis as sterling came under speculative pressure and its dollar reserves declined. The United States had the capacity to provide the financial assistance Britain required, but withheld support until the British government agreed to withdraw. The significance of Suez was not simply that Egypt could disrupt an important petroleum route, as Iran is doing now in the Strait of Hormuz. It was that Britain could no longer conduct an independent imperial military operation when the United States opposed it, because Washington could impose an external financial constraint that London could not escape. Suez did not create Britain’s monetary subordination. It made visible the hierarchy that had emerged through the two world wars. An equivalent moment for the United States would require another power capable of imposing a comparable external constraint on Washington. Disrupting international petroleum supplies is not by itself sufficient, in particular because the United States is not dependent on imports of energy commodities. The Global Fiat Dollar Standard and the Rise of China The history of international monetary standards reinforces the argument. The transition from Dutch to British hegemony coincided with the gradual displacement of silver by gold as the principal international monetary standard. The transition from British to American hegemony eventually produced a more radical transformation, namely, the demonetization of gold itself. The gold standard collapsed during the interwar crisis of the 1930s, although gold remained central to the international monetary arrangements established at Bretton Woods. Under that system, foreign monetary authorities could convert dollars into gold at a fixed price. When President Richard Nixon suspended dollar convertibility in August 1971, many observers expected American monetary predominance to decline. The United States could no longer guarantee the metallic backing of its international liabilities. Yet the dollar did not lose its position as the principal international currency. On the contrary, the eventual consolidation of the global fiat flexible dollar standard eliminated the requirement that the United States settle foreign official dollar claims in gold. The international monetary system remained organized around American liabilities but without the same metallic constraint. The aggressive reassertion of American monetary power in the early 1980s was central to the restoration of American hegemony, as Maria da Conceição Tavares argued at the time. Susan Strange similarly challenged the conventional view that American structural power was declining. The Volcker shock demonstrated the international consequences of American monetary power. The sharp increase in American interest rates helped produce the debt crisis of the developing world, forcing countries throughout Latin America and elsewhere into painful external adjustment. The aggressive reassertion of American monetary power in the early 1980s was central to the restoration of American hegemony. This history presents a serious problem for interpretations centered on the material backing of money or the pricing of particular commodities. The disappearance of gold convertibility did not end dollar predominance. The petrodollar arrangements of the 1970s reinforced an already existing monetary hierarchy. They did not create it. Together with the expansion of offshore dollar markets and private international banking, they helped consolidate what Peter Gowan called the Dollar-Wall Street Regime. Neither the deindustrialization of the United States nor the rise of Japan, the Asian Tigers, and China necessarily implies the end of American hegemony or of the international position of the dollar. The Dollar-Wall Street Regime survives even if the United States has been challenged in the productive arena. The distinction between productive and monetary predominance is essential for understanding the current international order. China has become a leading industrial power and an increasingly important source of advanced technology. In renewable energy, China clearly challenges the productive predominance long enjoyed by the United States. But China does not possess an equivalent position in international finance. The dollar remains the principal currency of international credit, foreign exchange trading, and official reserves. China itself continues to hold substantial dollar reserves, and much of its international lending and trade remains connected to the dollar system. The United States does not face a symmetrical dependence on the renminbi. This asymmetry is the foundation of American monetary privilege. The United States can finance international commitments and external liabilities in its own currency. Most other countries, including China, must continue to consider their access to the principal international currency. More importantly, the dollar’s position allows Washington to influence the external financial constraints faced by other countries. American sanctions can restrict access to international payment systems and financial markets. Conversely, the Federal Reserve can provide emergency dollar liquidity to selected foreign central banks, alleviating pressures that might otherwise produce financial crises. This ability to impose or relax external constraints is not simply an incidental benefit of the dollar’s international role. It is one of the central mechanisms through which monetary hierarchy sustains geopolitical power. China’s growing technological capabilities could certainly alter this balance over time. Dependence on Chinese strategic minerals, equipment, and manufacturing capacity already creates vulnerabilities for the United States. But dependence on particular imported commodities or technologies is different from financial dependence on another state’s currency. For a transformation comparable to the British-American transition, the United States would have to become dependent on Chinese-controlled resources or finance under conditions in which China could determine the terms of access. The emergence of substantial international borrowing, credit, and settlement in renminbi could form part of such a transformation, but nothing of the sort is in the cards in the near future. The Resilience of the Dollar None of this means that American monetary hegemony is permanent. China’s advances in batteries, electric vehicles, and renewable energy could erode American productive predominance, at least in some sectors. The increasing use of financial sanctions and other coercive measures may also encourage countries to develop alternatives to the dollar. But greater currency competition is not the same as a reversal of the underlying international financial hierarchy. Britain’s loss of monetary hegemony was ultimately tied not only to its dependence on American production but also to its reliance on dollar financing during the two world wars. Suez demonstrated that Washington could use that dependence to constrain British policy. The United States, by contrast, does not need to borrow in renminbi to sustain its international commitments, and China cannot yet impose a comparable external financial constraint on Washington. China’s challenge to American productive predominance is real, but no significant decline in the dollar’s international market share has occurred. Even if such a decline were to take place, it would not by itself establish a new monetary hegemon. Indeed, as America’s productive lead and the legitimacy of its international leadership erode, its reliance on sanctions, financial exclusion, and military pressure may increase. The problem may therefore be less the imminent disappearance of American monetary hegemony than its increasingly coercive character. The transition away from fossil fuels is essential for addressing climate change and could substantially reduce the external vulnerabilities of oil-importing countries. But it will not automatically create an alternative international monetary order. To paraphrase John Connally’s famous dictum, the dollar remains America’s currency and the rest of the world’s problem.
